unit.can_do_en: ask what something costs and pay by card or cash.

brief.situation_en: Maria buys strawberries from Pekka's stall at the market square.

lines.speaker: Pekka
lines.gloss_en: Hi! What can I get you?

judge.reason: Moi/hei and sulle/sinulle are register variants; same greeting and question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Hi! How much are those strawberries?

judge.reason: Paljonks/paljonko, noi/nuo, maksaa/maksavat are colloquial variants; same question about the price of those strawberries.
Viis euroo is spoken for viisi euroa; same price, five euros per litre.
Toi is colloquial for tuo; same meaning.
Euroo is spoken for euroa; same three euros.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Mä otan litran. Voinks mä maksaa kortilla?
lines.text_kirja: Minä otan litran. Voinko minä maksaa kortilla?
lines.gloss_en: I'll take a litre. Can I pay by card?

judge.reason: Mä/minä and voinks/voinko are register differences; same litre and card payment.

puhe.text: Mä otan litran. Voinks mä maksaa kortilla?

kirja.text: Minä otan litran. Voinko minä maksaa kortilla?

lines.speaker: Pekka
lines.gloss_en: Yes, of course. Here you go.

judge.reason: Joo and kyllä both mean yes; rest is identical.
Kiitti/kiitos and moikka/näkemiin are register variants of thanks and goodbye.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
Sinä with -lle for 'to, for'. Speech shortens it to sulle.
Paljon with the question ending -ko asks 'how much?'. Speech uses -ks: paljonks.
Nuo means those. Speech says noi.
Mansikka with -t for more than one, and kk turns to k: mansikat.
Books write maksavat when more than one thing costs. Speech keeps maksaa for one or many.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
Speech drops the final i: viisi becomes viis.
After a number the noun takes the partitive: neljä euroa. Speech turns -oa into -oo.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Tuo means that. Speech says toi.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Ottaa, to take, with -n for 'I'. The tt becomes t: otan.
Litra with -n when you take the whole thing: otan litran.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 1st person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Voin, I can, with -ko to ask. Speech says -ks: voinks.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Kortti with -lla for 'with, by', and tt turns to t: kortilla.
Joo is the everyday spoken yes. Books write kyllä.
From tosi, true. Totta kai means of course.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Tämä, this, with -ssä for 'in': tässä. Said when handing something over.
Kiitti is the everyday spoken thanks. Books write kiitos.
Näkemiin is the polite goodbye. In everyday speech people say moikka instead.
